pages.title: Other in-place array tricks
pages.summary: Reversal for rotations, using indices as hash keys, and sign marking — the O(1)-space tricks interviewers ask for as follow-ups.

pages.title: Read pointer and write pointer — in-place compaction
pages.summary: One index reads every element; a second index marks where the next kept element should be written. Removes, filters and deduplicates in O(n) time and O(1) space.

pages.title: Single pass with running state
pages.summary: Walk the array once, carrying a few variables that summarise everything seen so far — running sums, counters that reset, best-so-far.

pages.title: Binary numbers and bitwise operators
pages.summary: How integers look in binary, the six bitwise operators, shifts, and two's complement for negative numbers.

pages.title: Common bit tricks
pages.summary: n & (n−1) clears the lowest set bit, power-of-two checks, counting set bits, and enumerating subsets with masks.

pages.title: Counting bits for every number — a bit DP
pages.summary: bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1), or bits(i) = bits(i & (i − 1)) + 1. Fills the answer for 0..n in O(n).

pages.title: XOR tricks
pages.summary: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so XOR-ing everything cancels pairs. Single number, missing number, swap without a temp, and finding two unique numbers.

pages.title: Binary search — the invariant that makes it correct
pages.summary: Keep a range [lo, hi] that is guaranteed to contain the answer if it exists; halve it each step by comparing with the middle. O(log n).

pages.title: lower_bound and upper_bound — first ≥ and first >
pages.summary: The two boundary searches that solve insert position, first/last occurrence and counting in a sorted array.

pages.title: The "first true" template — one binary search for everything
pages.summary: Turn any monotone yes/no question into F…FT…T and find the first T with a half-open loop. Avoids every off-by-one decision.

pages.title: Binary search on the answer
pages.summary: When the question is "smallest X that works" and "works" is monotone in X, binary search over the value of X and test each guess with an O(n) check.

pages.title: Peaks and unimodal arrays
pages.summary: Binary search works without full sortedness: if a[mid] < a[mid+1], a peak exists to the right. Compare neighbours instead of a target.

pages.title: Binary search on rotated sorted arrays
pages.summary: After rotation one half around mid is always sorted; check whether the target lies in that sorted half to decide which half to keep.

sections.title: Template: search in rotated array (distinct values)

pages.title: Inorder of a BST is sorted
pages.summary: Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in increasing order — k-th smallest, validation, two-sum on a BST and conversion to a sorted list all follow.

pages.title: The BST invariant and validating it
pages.summary: Every node's value is greater than everything in its left subtree and less than everything in its right subtree — not just its children. Validate by passing a (low, high) range down.

pages.title: Using BST order — LCA and range queries
pages.summary: In a BST, the LCA of p and q is the first node whose value lies between them. Range sums and trims prune entire subtrees by comparing with the bounds.

pages.title: BST search, insert and delete
pages.summary: Search and insert follow one path down by comparing values. Delete has three cases: leaf, one child, two children (replace with the inorder successor).

pages.title: Avoiding duplicate results in backtracking
pages.summary: Sort the input; at one recursion level, skip a value equal to the one just tried. Produces each distinct subset or combination exactly once.

pages.title: Backtracking II — choosing the next element with a for-loop (combinations)
pages.summary: At each level, loop over which element to add next, starting from a start index so combinations are not repeated in different orders. Pass i to allow reuse, i+1 to forbid it.

pages.title: Backtracking on a grid (Word Search)
pages.summary: DFS from every cell, matching one character per step; mark the cell as used on the way in and restore it on the way out so other paths can use it.

pages.title: Backtracking III — permutations with a used array
pages.summary: At each position, try every element not yet used. A boolean used[] array (or swapping) tracks availability. n! results.

pages.title: Backtracking I — pick or skip (subsets)
pages.summary: At index i, either include a[i] in the current choice or not, and recurse to i+1. Every leaf is one subset. Choose → recurse → undo.

pages.title: Pruning — cutting branches that cannot succeed
pages.summary: Check validity before recursing, use sortedness to break early, and maintain O(1) constraint checks so whole subtrees are skipped.

pages.title: Choosing between array, unordered_map and map
pages.summary: A decision rule for picking the counting/lookup container, with speed, order and key-type trade-offs.

pages.title: Integer overflow — int, long long and where sums blow up
pages.summary: Ranges of int and long long, the operations that overflow in DSA problems, and safe patterns like mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

pages.title: The <algorithm> functions worth knowing
pages.summary: lower_bound, upper_bound, accumulate, max_element, reverse, iota, fill, unique and next_permutation — what each does and what it costs.

sections.title: Turning an iterator into an index

pages.title: map and set — the ordered containers
pages.summary: Balanced-tree containers with O(log n) operations, sorted iteration, lower_bound/upper_bound, and multiset for duplicates.

pages.title: pair, tuple and structured bindings
pages.summary: Bundling values into pairs, how pairs sort, and reading them cleanly with auto [a, b].

pages.title: Pass by value, reference and const reference
pages.summary: What each parameter style copies, why by-value vectors in recursion are a hidden O(n²), and lambdas capturing by reference.

pages.title: priority_queue — C++'s heap
pages.summary: Max-heap by default, how to make a min-heap, heaps of pairs, and custom comparators (with their reversed logic).

pages.title: Recursion depth and stack limits
pages.summary: How deep recursion can go before crashing, which problems hit the limit, and how to convert to iteration.

pages.title: sort and custom comparators
pages.summary: Sorting ranges, sorting by a key, writing comparators with lambdas, stability, and the strict-weak-ordering rule that causes crashes.

pages.title: stack, queue and deque in C++
pages.summary: The three sequence adaptors, their O(1) operations, and when a deque replaces both.

pages.title: C++ string — characters, indexing and the costs that bite
pages.summary: Strings as vectors of chars, character arithmetic, building strings efficiently, substr cost, and conversions.

pages.title: unordered_map and unordered_set — API and gotchas
pages.summary: Inserting, looking up, counting and erasing in hash containers, and the [] operator side effect that causes silent bugs.

pages.title: C++ vector — the container you will use in every problem
pages.summary: Declaring, filling, accessing and passing vectors; size and capacity; the operations that are secretly O(n).

pages.title: Amortised analysis — why "sometimes expensive" can still be O(1)
pages.summary: How to count total work across a whole sequence of operations, with the vector push_back, two-stack queue and monotonic stack examples.

sections.title: The counting trick: charge each element

pages.title: Big-O — counting work the way interviewers do
pages.summary: What O(·) means, how to count operations from code, the dominant-term rule, and the common complexities ranked.

pages.title: Reading n — converting constraints into a target complexity
pages.summary: The 10⁸ operations-per-second rule and the table that maps n to the complexity you must hit.

sections.title: How to use it in an OA

pages.title: Complexity of recursive code
pages.summary: Counting calls × work per call, the recursion tree picture, and the three results you need without the full master theorem.

pages.title: Space complexity and "in-place"
pages.summary: Auxiliary vs total space, what "O(1) extra space" and "in-place" really allow, and how recursion uses space.

pages.title: 0/1 knapsack — each item at most once
pages.summary: dp[c] = best (or whether possible, or number of ways) using items so far with capacity/sum c. For each item, loop c downwards: dp[c] = combine(dp[c], dp[c − w]).

pages.title: 1D DP on a line — take or skip, ways to reach
pages.summary: dp[i] depends on a fixed number of earlier states: climbing stairs (sum of ways), house robber (take or skip), decode ways (one or two digits).

pages.title: Bitmask DP (recognition level)
pages.summary: When n ≤ 20, a subset of items fits in an integer mask; dp[mask] = answer for that subset. O(2ⁿ · n).

pages.title: Counting DP vs optimising DP — and loop order
pages.summary: Counting adds over choices and starts from dp[0] = 1; optimising takes min/max and starts from 0 or infinity. For counting, the loop order decides whether order matters.

pages.title: Edit distance
pages.summary: dp[i][j] = minimum operations to turn a's first i characters into b's first j. Match → dp[i−1][j−1]; else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).

sections.title: How to remember the three moves

pages.title: Grid DP — paths moving right and down
pages.summary: dp[r][c] depends on the cell above and the cell to the left. Count paths (sum), minimum path sum (min), obstacles (zero out), squares (min of three neighbours + 1).

pages.title: Interval DP (recognition level)
pages.summary: dp[i][j] = answer for the subarray i..j, computed from smaller intervals by choosing a split point k. Burst balloons, matrix chain, palindrome partitioning. O(n³).

pages.title: Two-string DP — longest common subsequence
pages.summary: dp[i][j] = answer for the prefixes a[0..i) and b[0..j). If the last characters match, extend dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string.

pages.title: Longest increasing subsequence
pages.summary: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with a[j] < a[i]. O(n²); patience sorting with binary search gives O(n log n).

pages.title: Memoisation vs tabulation
pages.summary: Top-down (recursion + cache) and bottom-up (fill a table in order) compute the same states. Start top-down when the recursion is clearer; convert to bottom-up for speed and space optimisation.

pages.title: Space optimisation — keeping only the rows you need
pages.summary: If dp[i] only reads dp[i−1] (and dp[i−2]), keep a few variables or two rows instead of the whole table. In knapsack, iterating capacity backwards lets one row suffice.

sections.title: Two rows / one row for grids

pages.title: Designing the DP state
pages.summary: The state must contain exactly the information needed to make the remaining decisions optimally. If the transition needs to know something the state does not say, add a dimension.

sections.title: "Best in prefix" vs "best ending at i"

pages.title: State machine DP — the stock problems
pages.summary: Model each day as being in one of a few modes (holding, not holding, cooling down) with transitions between them; dp[mode] holds the best profit in that mode.

pages.title: Partition DP on strings — word break
pages.summary: dp[i] = can the first i characters be split into dictionary words? dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j..i) in the dictionary.

pages.title: Unbounded knapsack — coins you can reuse
pages.summary: Items can be used any number of times; loop capacity upwards. Coin change (minimum coins) and coin change II (number of combinations).

pages.title: What dynamic programming is
pages.summary: DP = recursion + remembering answers. It applies when the same subproblems repeat (overlap) and the best answer is built from best answers to subproblems (optimal substructure).

pages.title: Greedy with running balance (gas station, parentheses with wildcards)
pages.summary: Track a running surplus; when it goes negative, the current start is impossible and the next index becomes the new start. Or track a range [low, high] of possible balances.

pages.title: Intervals II — sort by end, keep the earliest finisher
pages.summary: To keep the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals (or remove the minimum), sort by end time and greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept end.

sections.title: Why sort by end, not by start

pages.title: Intervals I — sort by start and merge
pages.summary: Sort intervals by start; each next interval either overlaps the last merged one (extend its end) or starts a new block.

pages.title: Greedy reach — Jump Game I and II
pages.summary: Track the farthest index reachable so far; for minimum jumps, treat each jump as a BFS level whose range is [current end + 1, farthest].

pages.title: Greedy algorithms and how to trust them
pages.summary: Make the locally best choice and never revisit it. Correct only when an exchange argument shows the greedy choice can always be part of an optimal answer.

sections.title: How to test a greedy idea quickly

pages.title: Bellman–Ford and shortest paths with at most k edges
pages.summary: Relax every edge n−1 times; after round i, dist holds the shortest paths using at most i edges. Copying dist each round enforces the "at most k stops" limit.

pages.title: Breadth-first search — shortest paths in unweighted graphs
pages.summary: Explore vertices in order of distance from the source using a queue. The first time a vertex is reached is along a shortest path.

pages.title: Bipartite check — two-colouring
pages.summary: Colour the start vertex 0, every neighbour the opposite colour; a neighbour that already has the same colour proves the graph is not bipartite. Run from every uncoloured vertex.

pages.title: Connected components
pages.summary: Loop over every vertex; each unvisited one starts a new DFS/BFS that marks its whole component. The number of starts is the number of components.

pages.title: Cycle detection — undirected and directed
pages.summary: Undirected: a visited neighbour that is not your parent means a cycle. Directed: a neighbour that is still on the current DFS path (state "visiting") means a cycle.

pages.title: Depth-first search on graphs
pages.summary: Go as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. A visited array prevents infinite loops. O(n + m).

pages.title: Dijkstra's algorithm — shortest paths with non-negative weights
pages.summary: Repeatedly finalise the closest unfinalised vertex using a min-heap, and relax its edges. O((n + m) log n). Fails with negative edges.

pages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union)
pages.summary: Each set is a tree with a root representative. find follows parents to the root (with path compression); union links roots (by size or rank). Nearly O(1) per operation.

pages.title: Floyd–Warshall — all-pairs shortest paths (recognition level)
pages.summary: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) for every intermediate k. O(n³), n ≤ ~400.

pages.title: Grids as graphs — flood fill
pages.summary: Each cell is a vertex; its 4 neighbours are edges. DFS/BFS from a cell marks its whole region. Counting starts = counting islands.

pages.title: Implicit graphs — BFS over states
pages.summary: When vertices are states (words, lock combinations, board positions) and edges are allowed moves, generate neighbours on the fly and BFS for the minimum number of moves.

pages.title: Minimum spanning tree — Kruskal and Prim (recognition level)
pages.summary: Connect all vertices with minimum total edge weight. Kruskal: sort edges, add each one that joins two different components (DSU). Prim: grow from a vertex with a min-heap.

pages.title: Multi-source BFS
pages.summary: Push every source into the queue at time 0 and run one BFS; each cell's distance is to its nearest source. Rotting oranges, distance to nearest 0, walls and gates.

pages.title: Representing graphs — edge lists, adjacency lists, matrices
pages.summary: Vertices and edges, directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted, and how to build an adjacency list from the input format LeetCode gives you.

pages.title: Bridges and articulation points — Tarjan (recognition level)
pages.summary: An edge is a bridge if removing it disconnects the graph. DFS with discovery times and low-links finds all bridges in O(n + m).

pages.title: Topological sort — ordering with dependencies
pages.summary: Order the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so every edge points forward. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes a vertex with in-degree 0.

pages.title: Boyer–Moore voting — the majority element in O(1) space
pages.summary: Pair off different values against each other; the value that appears more than n/2 times always survives. One pass, two variables.

pages.title: Collisions — chaining vs open addressing
pages.summary: Why collisions are unavoidable and the two standard ways of handling them, with their trade-offs.

pages.title: Complement lookup — store what you have seen, look up what you need
pages.summary: For each element compute the partner it needs, ask a hash map whether that partner has already appeared, then record the element. Turns pair search from O(n²) into O(n).

sections.title: The order rule: check before insert

pages.title: Grouping by a derived key
pages.summary: Compute a canonical key for each item so that items that "belong together" share a key, then group them in a map from key to list.

pages.title: Frequency counting
pages.summary: Count how many times each value occurs in one pass, then answer questions about counts — anagrams, majority, duplicates, first unique.

pages.title: Load factor, rehashing and reserve
pages.summary: How the table grows to keep buckets short, why that keeps inserts O(1) amortised, and how reserve avoids the cost.

pages.title: Hash set membership and the start-of-run trick
pages.summary: Put all values in a set so membership is O(1), then only start counting a run from values whose predecessor is missing — finding the longest consecutive run in O(n).

pages.title: How a hash table works inside
pages.summary: Hash function, bucket array, and why lookup is O(1) on average — the mechanism behind unordered_map.

sections.title: What a good hash function does

pages.title: How a binary heap works
pages.summary: A complete binary tree stored in an array, where each parent is ≥ its children. Push sifts up, pop moves the last element to the root and sifts down. O(log n) each.

pages.title: K-way merge with a heap
pages.summary: Merge k sorted lists by keeping the current head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its successor. O(N log k).

pages.title: Top k with a heap of size k
pages.summary: To keep the k largest, use a MIN-heap of size k: its top is the smallest of the k largest, and anything smaller than it can be discarded. O(n log k).

pages.title: Two heaps — running median
pages.summary: A max-heap holds the smaller half, a min-heap the larger half; keep their sizes within one. The median is read from the tops in O(1); each insert is O(log n).

pages.title: Heap vs quickselect vs sort for k-th element
pages.summary: When to choose each approach for k-th largest, and what to say about their worst cases.

sections.title: What to say in an interview

pages.title: Kadane's algorithm — maximum subarray sum
pages.summary: At each index decide: extend the best subarray ending at the previous index, or start fresh here. cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur).

pages.title: Maximum product subarray — tracking max and min together
pages.summary: A negative number turns the smallest product into the largest, so keep both the max and the min product ending here.

pages.title: Best partner to the left — min so far
pages.summary: For pair problems "j > i, maximise a[j] − a[i]", the best i for each j is simply the smallest value seen before j. Keep one running minimum.

pages.title: The dummy (sentinel) head
pages.summary: A fake node placed before the real head so that inserting or deleting at the front is no longer a special case. Return dummy.next.

pages.title: Fast and slow pointers
pages.summary: One pointer moves one step, the other two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; if there is a cycle, they meet inside it.

pages.title: Floyd's cycle algorithm — finding where the cycle starts
pages.summary: After slow and fast meet, a pointer from the head and a pointer from the meeting point, both moving one step, meet exactly at the cycle's entry. Here is why.

pages.title: Two pointers with a k-node gap
pages.summary: Advance a lead pointer k steps, then move both together; when the lead hits the end, the trailing pointer is k from the end. Removes the n-th node from the end in one pass.

pages.title: Merging, splitting and comparing lists
pages.summary: Merge two sorted lists with a dummy head; split a list at its middle; combine split + reverse + compare for palindromes; merge sort for lists.

pages.title: Linked list nodes and pointer manipulation
pages.summary: What a ListNode is, how next pointers chain nodes, traversal, and the rule for changing pointers without losing the rest of the list.

pages.title: Reversing a linked list
pages.summary: Walk the list with prev, cur and next, flipping each pointer to point backwards. Iterative O(1) space; recursive version for understanding.

pages.title: In-place marking in matrices
pages.summary: Use the first row and column (or a sentinel value) as storage to mark rows/columns, achieving O(1) extra space.

pages.title: Rotating a matrix — transpose then reverse
pages.summary: Rotate 90° clockwise in place = transpose (swap across the main diagonal) + reverse each row.

pages.title: Spiral order — shrinking boundaries
pages.summary: Keep top, bottom, left, right boundaries; walk the four sides of the current layer and shrink the boundaries after each side.

pages.title: Matrix traversal and direction arrays
pages.summary: Rows, columns, bounds checks, the dr/dc direction arrays for neighbours, and flattening (r, c) into one index.

sections.title: Flattening a cell to an index

pages.title: GCD, LCM and modular arithmetic
pages.summary: Euclid's algorithm, LCM without overflow, and the rules for adding and multiplying modulo 10⁹+7.

pages.title: Primes and the sieve of Eratosthenes
pages.summary: Trial division up to √n for one number; the sieve marks multiples of each prime to find all primes below n in O(n log log n).

pages.title: Analysing a problem before you think of an algorithm
pages.summary: The five questions to answer on paper before any idea of a solution — what goes in, what comes out, what the constraints allow, what a tiny example shows, and what makes it hard.

sections.title: Why analysis is a separate step
How to use the tiny example
The analysis box (copy this layout onto paper)

pages.title: The bottleneck method — getting from brute force to optimal
pages.summary: A repeatable way to improve a solution: write the brute force, find the single line doing the most wasted work, name why it is wasted, and pick the tool that removes exactly that waste.

sections.title: Step 1: always write the brute force
Step 3: name why the work is wasted
Questions that unlock the next step
Worked example: three steps on one problem

pages.title: Dry runs — tracing variables by hand
pages.summary: How to trace pseudocode on a small input in a table, so bugs show up on paper instead of in submissions.

pages.title: The pattern decision tree — from keywords and constraints to a technique
pages.summary: The master map to read before every mock OA: which words, constraints and shapes in a problem point to which pattern, with the page to read for each.

sections.title: Then the shape of the input
Then the words in the question

pages.title: Writing pseudocode — the 5-slot format
pages.summary: A fixed layout (state, loop, check, update, return) that turns an idea into pseudocode you can translate to C++ line by line, so you never face a blank page.

sections.title: Algorithm in words first, then pseudocode
Style rules that make translation mechanical
Example: Two Sum in five slots

pages.title: 2D prefix sums — rectangle sums in O(1)
pages.summary: P[r][c] = sum of the rectangle from (0,0) to (r−1,c−1); any sub-rectangle sum is four lookups with inclusion–exclusion.

pages.title: Prefix sums modulo k
pages.summary: A subarray's sum is divisible by k exactly when the two bounding prefixes have the same remainder mod k — count equal remainders.

pages.title: Prefix and suffix passes — everything except me
pages.summary: Answer "combine everything to my left with everything to my right" with one left-to-right pass and one right-to-left pass, without division.

sections.title: Template: product except self in O(1) extra space

pages.title: Prefix sums — any range sum in O(1)
pages.summary: Precompute pre[i] = sum of the first i elements; then the sum of a[l..r] is pre[r+1] − pre[l]. One O(n) pass turns every range-sum query into O(1).

pages.title: Prefix sum + hash map — counting subarrays with a given sum
pages.summary: A subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when pre[j] − pre[i] = k. Walk once with a running prefix sum and count how many earlier prefixes equal pre[j] − k, using a map seeded with {0: 1}.

pages.title: Divide and conquer
pages.summary: Split the problem into independent smaller parts, solve them recursively, combine. Fast power and merge sort are the two models.

sections.title: Merge sort as the second model

pages.title: How recursion works — base case, call stack and the leap of faith
pages.summary: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. Define what it returns, handle the smallest case, and trust the recursive call.

pages.title: The recursion tree — seeing the cost of recursion
pages.summary: Draw each call as a node and its recursive calls as children; the number of nodes is the number of calls, the height is the stack depth.

pages.title: Counting sort and bucket ideas
pages.summary: When values lie in a small range, count occurrences and rebuild the array in O(n + range). Bucket-by-frequency gives O(n) top-k.

pages.title: Dutch national flag — three-way partition in one pass
pages.summary: Three pointers split the array into < pivot, = pivot, unknown, > pivot regions; one pass sorts 0s, 1s and 2s in place.

pages.title: Merge sort
pages.summary: Split in half, sort each half recursively, merge the two sorted halves with two pointers. O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space.

pages.title: Quick sort, partitioning and quickselect
pages.summary: Partition around a pivot so smaller elements go left, then recurse on both sides. O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst case with bad pivots; quickselect finds the k-th element in O(n) average.

pages.title: Stability and the n log n lower bound
pages.summary: What stability means and when it matters, and why comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n) — but counting sort can.

pages.title: Designing with an auxiliary stack (Min Stack)
pages.summary: Store extra information alongside each element — the minimum so far — so queries about the whole stack stay O(1) after any push or pop.

pages.title: Evaluating expressions with stacks
pages.summary: Reverse Polish notation is evaluated with one operand stack; infix expressions use a stack of partial results and signs.

pages.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
pages.summary: Each bar's best rectangle spans to the nearest smaller bar on each side. A monotonic increasing stack finds both boundaries in one pass.

pages.title: Monotonic deque — maximum of every window
pages.summary: Keep window indices in a deque with decreasing values; the front is the window maximum. Pop the back when a bigger element arrives, pop the front when it leaves the window.

pages.title: Monotonic stack — next greater and previous smaller
pages.summary: Keep a stack whose values are always decreasing (or increasing). When a new element breaks the order, it is the "next greater" for every element it pops. O(n) total.

pages.title: Queue from two stacks — amortised O(1)
pages.summary: Push into an input stack; pop from an output stack, refilling it from the input only when it is empty. Every element moves at most once.

pages.title: Stacks — last in, first out, and bracket matching
pages.summary: A stack remembers unfinished things in reverse order, so the most recent opener is matched first. Valid parentheses, undo, nested structures.

pages.title: Anagram windows — finding permutations inside a string
pages.summary: A fixed window of size |p| sliding over s, with 26 counts compared against p's counts — or a single "matches" counter for O(1) comparison.

sections.title: The O(1) comparison: a matches counter

pages.title: Characters as numbers — counting, mapping and comparing
pages.summary: Using c − 'a' as an index, case handling, scanning several strings column by column, and comparing strings character by character.

sections.title: Vertical scanning: many strings at once

pages.title: Expand around center — longest palindromic substring
pages.summary: Every palindrome has a center (a character or a gap between two). Try all 2n−1 centers and expand while both sides match. O(n²) time, O(1) space.

pages.title: KMP and the prefix function (recognition level)
pages.summary: Linear-time pattern matching using, for each prefix, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. Know what it is and when it is needed; code it only if asked.

pages.title: Palindrome checks
pages.summary: Two-pointer palindrome checks, skipping non-alphanumeric characters, and the "delete at most one character" extension.

pages.title: Rolling hash (recognition level)
pages.summary: Represent a substring as a number that can be updated in O(1) when the window slides, to compare substrings in O(1) (Rabin–Karp).

pages.title: Splitting into words and reversing
pages.summary: Extracting words while skipping extra spaces, reversing word order, and the in-place reverse-twice trick.

pages.title: Exactly k = at most k minus at most (k − 1)
pages.summary: "Exactly k" conditions are not monotone, but "at most k" is. Count windows for at most k and at most k−1 and subtract.

pages.title: Fixed-size sliding window
pages.summary: For every window of exactly k consecutive elements, update the window's summary in O(1) by adding the element that enters and removing the one that leaves.

pages.title: Windows with a frequency map
pages.summary: Keep the counts of everything inside the window; update one count on each add and remove; validity is a question about those counts.

pages.title: When a sliding window works — and when it breaks
pages.summary: Windows need a monotone condition: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid. Negative numbers in sum problems break this, which is why prefix sums are needed there.

pages.title: Variable-size sliding window — expand right, shrink left
pages.summary: Grow the window by moving right one step at a time; whenever the window breaks a rule, shrink from the left until it is valid again. Each index enters and leaves once, so it is O(n).

sections.title: The "budget" form: at most k bad things

pages.title: Fix one, two-pointer the rest (3Sum, 4Sum)
pages.summary: Sort, loop over the first element, and solve the remaining 2-sum on the suffix with two pointers. Reduces k-sum from O(n^k) to O(n^(k-1)).

pages.title: Two pointers from opposite ends
pages.summary: Put one pointer at each end of a sorted array (or a string), and move whichever pointer the comparison tells you to. Each step discards one candidate forever, so the scan is O(n).

sections.title: Template: pair sum on sorted array

pages.title: Skipping duplicates in sorted scans
pages.summary: The three dedup idioms — compare with the previous element at a loop start, skip runs after a hit, and the i > start rule in backtracking.

pages.title: Why moving a pointer is safe — the exchange argument
pages.summary: The proof that two-pointer scans do not skip the answer, for pair-sum and for Container With Most Water, phrased so you can say it in an interview.

sections.title: The argument for Container With Most Water
How to say it in an interview

pages.title: Treating a tree as a graph — parent pointers
pages.summary: Record each node's parent with one DFS, then BFS from the target in three directions (left, right, parent) to find nodes at distance k.

pages.title: BFS level order — processing a tree level by level
pages.summary: A queue visits nodes in order of depth. Reading q.size() at the start of each round gives exactly one level, which solves level lists, right side view, averages and zigzags.

pages.title: Bottom-up recursion — returning answers from subtrees
pages.summary: Define what the function returns for a subtree, get it for both children, combine into the answer for the current node. Height, size, balanced, sums.

pages.title: Building a tree from preorder and inorder
pages.summary: Preorder's first element is the root; its position in inorder splits the left and right subtrees. Recurse with index ranges and a value → index map.

pages.title: DFS traversals — preorder, inorder, postorder
pages.summary: Three orders that differ only in when the node itself is processed relative to its subtrees. Which one you need depends on whether the node's answer needs its children's answers.

pages.title: Return one thing, record another — the global answer pattern
pages.summary: When the best answer can bend through a node (diameter, max path sum), the function returns the best straight downward path, while a global variable records the best bent path through each node.

pages.title: Iterative traversals with an explicit stack
pages.summary: Replace the call stack with your own: inorder pushes all left children then visits; preorder pops and pushes right before left.

pages.title: Lowest common ancestor in a binary tree
pages.summary: Return the node if it is p or q; otherwise ask both subtrees. If both return non-null, this node is the LCA; else pass up whichever is non-null.

sections.title: Why returning early at p is correct

pages.title: Serialising and deserialising a tree (recognition level)
pages.summary: Write a preorder traversal with explicit null markers; read it back with the same recursion. The null markers make the shape unambiguous.

pages.title: Binary trees — terms and representation
pages.summary: Nodes, root, leaves, depth vs height, complete/full/balanced trees, and the TreeNode struct you will use everywhere.

pages.title: Top-down recursion — passing information down
pages.summary: Pass what the node needs from above (running sum, depth, current path, allowed range) as parameters. Root-to-leaf path problems use choose → recurse → undo on a path vector.

sections.title: Template: all root-to-leaf paths with sum

pages.title: Tries — prefix trees
pages.summary: A tree where each edge is a character and each root-to-node path spells a prefix. Insert, search and startsWith all cost O(word length).

pages.title: Trie search with wildcards (DFS over children)
pages.summary: A '.' matches any letter, so at that position try every existing child recursively. Normal letters follow one child.
